nameStory: Round hornwort gets its name from the distinctive horn-shaped spore capsules that stick up from the plant like tiny green horns. The 'round' part refers to the circular, disk-like shape of the plant body (called a thallus) that spreads flat against the ground. It's like nature's version of a green pancake with little horns poking up!
description: Round hornwort is a tiny, primitive plant called a hornwort that looks nothing like the aquatic hornworts you might know from fish tanks. Instead, this little ground-hugger forms small, flat, circular discs about the size of a quarter or smaller that press tightly against moist soil. The most distinctive feature is the slender, horn-like structures that poke up from the green discs - these are the spore-producing capsules. You'll need to look closely to spot this miniature marvel, as it's easily overlooked among moss and other small plants.

idTips.label: Horn-like capsules
idTips.description: Look for slender, pointed green 'horns' about 1/2 inch tall sticking straight up from the plant body - these feel firm but slightly flexible when gently touched

idTips.label: Circular thallus
idTips.description: The plant body forms flat, round discs pressed against the soil, feeling smooth and slightly rubbery to the touch, like a thin green button

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Entire plant is tiny - usually less than an inch across, making it easy to overlook among other ground vegetation

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: The green disc surface appears smooth and somewhat glossy, without the leafy appearance of mosses or the lobed look of liverworts

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Often grows in small colonies of several round discs clustered together on bare or disturbed soil

habitat: Round hornwort favors disturbed, moist soil in open areas like field edges, trail sides, and garden beds where competition from larger plants is limited. Look for it on clay or loamy soils that stay damp but not waterlogged, often in partially shaded spots. It's quite rare in New England, so finding it is a real treat for sharp-eyed plant hunters.

seasonality.spring: This is the best time to spot round hornwort as it begins active growth and the distinctive horn-like capsules start developing. The green discs are most vibrant and noticeable.
seasonality.summer: The horn-shaped spore capsules reach full development and may split open to release spores. Look for the characteristic pointed 'horns' standing tall above the flat green discs.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline but may still be visible. Spore capsules may appear brown or dried, and the green discs start to fade.
seasonality.winter: Generally not visible above ground in New England's cold climate, surviving as resistant spores or underground structures until spring returns.

funFact: Round hornwort has been around for over 300 million years, making it one of the most ancient plant lineages still alive today - it was already old when the first dinosaurs appeared!
confusionNotes: Round hornwort might be mistaken for small liverworts or baby moss plants, but those distinctive upright horn-shaped capsules are the dead giveaway - no moss or liverwort produces anything quite like these pointed green 'horns' sticking straight up.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this land-dwelling hornwort with the feathery aquatic hornworts sold for fish tanks - they're completely unrelated plants that just happen to share a common name due to their horn-shaped features.
compareHints: **Note: Identification details for this rare species should be verified with expert sources, as observation data is limited.** Round hornwort is the only Notothylas species reported in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other hornworts you might encounter, it's distinguished by its particularly small, round thallus and the way it forms neat circular discs rather than irregular lobed shapes.
